mentions.quote: the property of a god, a Brāhmaṇa, or a king are to be known as high-value objects
mentions.role: protected class whose property is highest-value

mentions.quote: A Kṣatriya who abuses a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred
mentions.role: victim in caste-graded defamation fines

mentions.quote: two are declared to be unspeakable and unpunishable: a Brāhmaṇa and the king
mentions.role: legally inviolable person

mentions.quote: With whatever limb a man of a lower class injures a Brāhmaṇa, that limb of his should be cut off
mentions.role: protected body against lower-caste assault

mentions.quote: The king should always serve Brāhmaṇas with a concentrated mind
mentions.role: recipient of royal service

mentions.quote: One should never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is involved in all sins
mentions.role: inviolable—exempt from capital punishment

mentions.quote: In the case of a Brāhmaṇa's four great sins, branding is prescribed
mentions.role: subject of branding as substitute punishment

mentions.quote: One should not give poison to a Brāhmaṇa
mentions.role: exempt from ordeal by poison

entities.description: The priestly class who enjoy supreme legal protection, exemption from capital punishment, and privileged ritual and social status throughout the Nāradasmṛti's penal and administrative rules.
entities.justification: Brāhmaṇas are the most frequently named social group in this window, with explicit legal exemptions, elevated fines for their abuse, and unique ritual privileges distinguishing them from all other varṇas.

mentions.quote: the king should pay from his own treasury. For if he is negligent, he becomes sinful
mentions.role: financially liable guarantor of public security

mentions.quote: Command is the power of kings, and that is established in their speech
mentions.role: source of law

mentions.quote: This one, called the king, moves on earth as the thousand-eyed one in person
mentions.role: divine embodiment on earth

mentions.quote: Kings of immeasurable power assume five forms: of Agni, of Indra, of Soma, of Yama, and of Dhanada
mentions.role: divine polymorph

mentions.quote: His duty is the protection of his subjects, attendance upon the aged and wise, the examination of legal disputes
mentions.role: obligated protector and judge

mentions.quote: The same amount of sin that a king incurs by executing one who should not be executed, he incurs by releasing one who should be executed
mentions.role: agent of just punishment

mentions.quote: A king who knows Dharma, who administers the five ordeals to the accused according to the stated manner, rejoices hereafter and in this world
mentions.role: administrator of divine ordeals

entities.description: The king is the central legal and quasi-divine authority in the Nāradasmṛti: source of law, guarantor of public order, embodiment of five divine forms, and personally responsible for both just punishment and the sin of unjust execution or release.
entities.justification: The king is invoked in nearly every major section of this window—from theft tracking and gambling regulation to the five divine forms and the ordeal procedures—marking him as the pivotal institutional and theological figure of the text.

mentions.quote: Kings of immeasurable power assume five forms: of Agni, of Indra, of Soma, of Yama, and of Dhanada
mentions.role: one of the five divine forms of the king

mentions.quote: When the king, with or without cause, overcome by anger, burns his subjects, then he is called Agni
mentions.role: wrathful form of the king

mentions.quote: You, O Fire, move within all beings as a witness. The good and evil deeds in the world, unknown to men, are known by you
mentions.role: omniscient divine witness in the ordeal ritual

mentions.quote: Just as fire is not tainted while constantly burning these creatures, so a king is not tainted by inflicting punishment
mentions.role: analogical figure for the king's moral purity

entities.description: Agni (fire) functions both as one of the king's five divine manifestations and as the divine witness invoked in the ordeal by fire, into whose presence the accused carries a heated iron ball.
entities.justification: Agni is explicitly named as one of the king's five forms and is ritually invoked as an omniscient witness in the fire ordeal, making him a theologically active figure in both the governance and juridical sections of this window.

mentions.quote: Kings of immeasurable power assume five forms: of Agni, of Indra, of Soma, of Yama, and of Dhanada
mentions.role: one of the five divine forms of the king

mentions.quote: When the king, having taken up his brilliant power, desirous of victory and with weapons raised, attacks his enemies, then he is called Indra
mentions.role: martial, victorious form of the king

mentions.quote: This one, called the king, moves on earth as the thousand-eyed one in person
mentions.role: epithet applied to the king on earth

entities.description: Indra, the storm-king of the gods and wielder of the thunderbolt, is invoked as the martial divine form assumed by the king when he goes to war, and his epithet 'thousand-eyed' is applied directly to the ruling monarch.
entities.justification: Indra is explicitly named among the king's five divine forms and his defining epithet is applied to the earthly king, giving him a textually active role in the theology of kingship in this window.

mentions.quote: Kings of immeasurable power assume five forms: of Agni, of Indra, of Soma, of Yama, and of Dhanada
mentions.role: one of the five divine forms of the king

mentions.quote: When the king, his anger and heat having passed, with a joyful appearance, grants an audience to his subjects, he is then called Soma
mentions.role: gentle, beneficent form of the king

entities.description: Soma, the lunar deity and ritual drink, represents the king's gentle, favour-granting aspect when he receives subjects with a joyful appearance after anger has passed.
entities.justification: Soma is named as one of the king's five divine forms and is specifically elaborated as the king's benevolent, audience-granting manifestation in verse 18.27.

mentions.quote: Kings of immeasurable power assume five forms: of Agni, of Indra, of Soma, of Yama, and of Dhanada
mentions.role: one of the five divine forms of the king

mentions.quote: When the glorious king, seated on the throne of justice, wields the rod of punishment, being equal to all beings, then he is Yama Vaivasvata
mentions.role: just, impartial judge form of the king

mentions.quote: The guru is the chastiser of the self-controlled; the king is the chastiser of the wicked. And the chastiser of those with hidden sins is Yama Vaivasvata
mentions.role: post-mortem chastiser of hidden sinners

entities.description: Yama Vaivasvata, the god of death and cosmic justice, is both one of the king's five divine forms when he dispenses equal justice and the ultimate chastiser of sins hidden from earthly punishment.
entities.justification: Yama Vaivasvata is named twice in this window: once as the king's judicial divine form (18.28) and once as the chastiser of hidden sins beyond the reach of kings (19.57), giving him a distinct soteriological role.

mentions.quote: Kings of immeasurable power assume five forms: of Agni, of Indra, of Soma, of Yama, and of Dhanada
mentions.role: one of the five divine forms of the king

mentions.quote: When the lord of the earth bestows favor with gifts upon petitioners, gurus, the wise, servants, and others, then he is remembered as Dhanada
mentions.role: wealth-giving form of the king

entities.description: Dhanada (Kubera, lord of wealth) is the divine form assumed by the king when he bestows gifts and favours, representing the royal patronage dimension of sovereignty.
entities.justification: Dhanada is explicitly named as the fifth of the king's divine forms (18.24, 18.29), representing the gift-giving and patronage function of royal power.

mentions.quote: the punishment is death. For a lesser amount, he should be made to pay a fine of eleven times the value, so said Manu
mentions.role: cited authority for grain-theft penalty

mentions.quote: With whatever particular limb a thief operates, that very limb of his should be cut off; this is the ordinance of Manu
mentions.role: lawgiver source for mutilation punishment

mentions.quote: Manu Svāyaṃbhuva declared ten places of punishment, which should apply to the three classes; a Brāhmaṇa is always protected
mentions.role: source for the ten bodily sites of punishment

mentions.quote: A perpetrator of violence, who has abandoned his own self, should not be released by the king because of friendship or a large monetary gain, said Manu
mentions.role: cited authority against clemency for violent offenders

mentions.quote: This threefold punishment for crimes of violence was declared by the Self-existent One
mentions.role: divine source for the three-tier violence penalty

mentions.quote: For a Brāhmaṇa, it is sixty-fourfold; thus said Svāyaṃbhuva
mentions.role: cited source for graduated theft-sin scale

mentions.quote: the ordeal is known to be of five kinds, so says the blessed Manu
mentions.role: authority for the fivefold ordeal typology

entities.description: Manu Svāyaṃbhuva, the primordial lawgiver, is repeatedly cited in the Appendix section as the authoritative source for penalties on theft, mutilation rules, the ten sites of punishment, and the fivefold ordeal system.
entities.justification: Manu is the most frequently cited individual authority in this window, invoked seven times across sections on theft penalties, bodily punishments, and ordeals, establishing him as the primary external legal tradition the Nāradasmṛti appeals to.

mentions.quote: remembering the Dharma of Prajāpati for his servants; this is the established rule
mentions.role: divine authority for the king's treatment of Brāhmaṇa servants

entities.description: Prajāpati, the lord of creatures and primordial creator-deity, is invoked as the divine precedent for the rule that a king may take a Brāhmaṇa's property or leave him a quarter, following Prajāpati's Dharma for servants.
entities.justification: Prajāpati is explicitly named as the divine model (19.49) for the king's restrained treatment of Brāhmaṇa offenders, grounding a legal rule in cosmogonic authority.

mentions.quote: You, O Poison, are the son of Brahmā, established in truth and Dharma
mentions.role: divine progenitor of the ordeal poison

entities.description: Brahmā, the creator god, is invoked in the poison-ordeal invocation as the divine progenitor of the ordeal poison, legitimising its ritual use through cosmogonic lineage.
entities.justification: Brahmā is explicitly named in the liturgical formula of the poison ordeal (20.40), making his mention textually grounded and ritually significant.

mentions.quote: the means of distinguishing truth from untruth were again declared by the great-souled Nārada
mentions.role: attributed composer of the ordeal rules

mentions.quote: The Dharmaśāstra of Nārada is complete
mentions.role: named author of the entire work

entities.description: Nārada, the divine sage, is named as the author of the Dharmaśāstra and as the one who declared the means of distinguishing truth from falsehood through ordeals, appearing at the close of the text.
entities.justification: Nārada is named in the colophon as the work's author and is also invoked within the ordeal section (20.7) as its specific authority, grounding both the work's title and its juridical method in his name.

mentions.quote: In villages, the search should be conducted by Cāṇḍālas, executioners, and others
mentions.role: assigned agents for tracking thieves

mentions.quote: In the case of Śvapākas, eunuchs, Cāṇḍālas, the deformed, those who live by execution
mentions.role: member of the impure class exempt from assault-fault rules

entities.description: Cāṇḍālas are a ritually impure outcaste group assigned to carry out searches for thieves in villages and also listed among those whose transgression of propriety incurs immediate death rather than ordinary assault penalties.
entities.justification: Cāṇḍālas are mentioned in two distinct legal contexts—as designated search agents (14.25) and as members of a legally marginal class subject to extreme measures (15.12)—confirming their structural role in the text's social hierarchy.

mentions.quote: a Śūdra deserves death
mentions.role: subject of capital punishment for abusing a Brāhmaṇa

mentions.quote: For a Śūdra who, with intent to injure, takes the name and caste of the twice-born
mentions.role: subject of corporal punishment for caste impersonation

mentions.quote: The sin of a Śūdra in theft is eightfold
mentions.role: lowest multiplier in the graduated theft-sin scale

mentions.quote: a Śūdra should not be made to drink consecrated water
mentions.role: barred from the ordeal by consecrated water

entities.description: Śūdras, the lowest of the four varṇas, are subject to the harshest corporal penalties for verbal and physical transgressions against higher castes and bear an eightfold sin-multiplier for theft, while being excluded from the consecrated-water ordeal.
entities.justification: Śūdras appear across the verbal assault, physical assault, theft-sin scaling, and ordeal sections—each time in a legally disadvantaged position relative to the twice-born, making them a structurally defining group for the text's hierarchical legal logic.

mentions.quote: A Kṣatriya who abuses a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred
mentions.role: subject of caste-graded defamation fine

mentions.quote: The Kṣatra power, when united with the Brāhmaṇa power, is the root of the protection of the world
mentions.role: co-pillar of world protection with Brāhmaṇas

mentions.quote: nor should a Kṣatriya carry the iron
mentions.role: exempt from the fire ordeal

entities.description: Kṣatriyas, the warrior-ruler class, are liable to heavy fines for abusing Brāhmaṇas, ideologically paired with Brāhmaṇas as co-protectors of the world, and exempt from the fire ordeal.
entities.justification: Kṣatriyas appear in the defamation fine scale, the theological pairing with Brāhmaṇa power, and the ordeal exemption table, marking their distinct legal and cosmological position in this window.

mentions.quote: A Vaiśya, one hundred and fifty or two hundred
mentions.role: subject of caste-graded defamation fine for abusing a Brāhmaṇa

mentions.quote: a Vaiśya would abandon his own work
mentions.role: class that abandons its duty without royal enforcement

mentions.quote: A Vaiśya should not be submerged in water
mentions.role: exempt from the water ordeal

entities.description: Vaiśyas, the merchant-agricultural class, incur higher defamation fines than Kṣatriyas for abusing Brāhmaṇas, depend on royal enforcement to maintain their dharmic role, and are barred from the water ordeal.
entities.justification: Vaiśyas are named in three distinct legal-functional contexts—fines, social order, and ordeal exemptions—situating them within the text's four-varṇa structural logic.

mentions.quote: That from the Śṛṅga or Himavat mountains is praised, endowed with good smell, color, and taste
mentions.role: geographic source of the best ordeal poison

entities.description: Śṛṅga and Himavat (the Himalayan range) are named as the geographic sources of the highest-quality poison to be used in the ordeal by poison, distinguished by superior smell, colour, and taste.
entities.justification: These mountains are explicitly identified (20.35) as the provenance of the preferred ordeal poison, making them the only geographic place-entities introduced in this window.

themes.topic: Graduated punishment calibrated to caste rank and offence severity

mentions.quote: A Kṣatriya who abuses a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred. A Vaiśya, one hundred and fifty or two hundred; a Śūdra deserves death
The same punishment that has been stated by the wise for the three kinds of crimes of violence is also the punishment for theft, in order, for the three kinds of objects
The sin of a Śūdra in theft is eightfold. It is sixteenfold for a Vaiśya, and thirty-twofold for a Kṣatriya

themes.justification: Every major offence category in this window—theft, verbal assault, physical assault, and ordeal administration—applies penalties in strict proportion to both the caste of the offender and the value/gravity of the target, making graduated hierarchy the organising principle of the entire penal system.

themes.topic: Divine kingship: the king as embodiment of five deities and cosmic law

mentions.quote: Kings of immeasurable power assume five forms: of Agni, of Indra, of Soma, of Yama, and of Dhanada
This one, called the king, moves on earth as the thousand-eyed one in person
He at whose word an impure man becomes pure, and a pure man immediately becomes impure—how is the king not a divinity?

themes.justification: Chapter 18 develops an extended theology of kingship in which the monarch is not merely an administrator but a polymorph deity whose spoken word is law and whose five divine forms encompass the full spectrum from wrathful punishment to generous patronage.

themes.topic: Punishment as spiritual purification and transfer of sin

mentions.quote: Men who have committed sins, having been punished by kings, become pure and go to heaven, like good people who have done meritorious deeds
By this confession of his own deed, the thief becomes free from sin. That sin touches the king who releases the sinner
Whether by punishment or by release, a thief is freed from sin. But by not punishing, the king incurs the sin of the thief

themes.justification: The Appendix (ch. 19) explicitly frames royal punishment as a mechanism of karmic purification: the sinner is cleansed, while unexecuted sin transfers to the negligent king, giving the penal system a soteriological rationale beyond mere social control.

themes.topic: Ordeals (divya) as divine-juridical technology for truth-determination

mentions.quote: The balance, fire, and water, and poison, and the consecrated water as the fifth—these ordeals are declared for the purification of the accused
You are called 'Balance' by words that are synonyms for Dharma. You know the sins and meritorious deeds of all beings
You, O Fire, move within all beings as a witness. The good and evil deeds in the world, unknown to men, are known by you

themes.justification: The entire chapter 20 presents ordeals not as torture but as ritually sanctioned consultations with divine witnesses (fire, water, balance, poison) who have omniscient access to hidden truth, framing juridical uncertainty as a theological problem solved by ritual.

themes.topic: Complicity and collective liability in theft and robbery

mentions.quote: Those who give food and shelter to roaming thieves, and those who, though able, are indifferent, they too share in that guilt
the buyers of stolen goods and those who receive them—all these are remembered as deserving the same punishment as the thieves
The officials in the districts and the local chiefs, when called upon, who remain neutral during attacks, they are just like thieves

themes.justification: The theft sections (14 and 19) consistently extend criminal liability beyond the direct thief to harborers, bystanders, receivers, buyers, and negligent officials, constructing a wide network of collective responsibility.

themes.topic: Track-and-trace liability for stolen property recovery

mentions.quote: Wherever the track leads, in a village, a pasture, or a clearing, the responsibility for the stolen goods falls on that place
If the track is lost or broken, or is on uneven ground near a settlement, it should be traced to the nearest village or pasture
In whose pasture a theft occurs, he must diligently search for the thieves. Otherwise, he must pay for the theft, if the track does not lead out

themes.justification: Both sections 14 and 19 develop a detailed system of territorial liability anchored to the physical tracking of stolen goods, placing financial obligation on the locality or administrative unit where the trail ends—an early form of territorial culpability doctrine.

themes.topic: Brahminical privilege and special exemptions as structural legal axiom

mentions.quote: A Brāhmaṇa is not to be passed over; he has a seat in front of the king, the first audience in the morning
In taking sacrificial wood, flowers, and water, there is no theft, even from one who has property
One should never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is involved in all sins. He should be banished at will; this is the established law

themes.justification: Chapter 18 and the Appendix articulate a systematic set of Brahminical exemptions—from theft charges, from capital punishment, from certain ordeals—that function as structural axioms underpinning the entire legal code rather than mere ad hoc privileges.

themes.topic: Verbal and physical assault as parallel, symmetrically structured offences

mentions.quote: Abusive language connected with insults to one's country, caste, family, and the like, which has a hostile meaning, is called verbal assault
An attack on another's body with hands, feet, weapons, and the like, and injury with ashes and the like, is called physical assault
A fivefold rule is stated for both of these, as to how acquittal and liability to punishment are connected there

themes.justification: Chapters 15 and 16 are structurally mirrored—each defines its offence, grades it into three sub-types, and then applies a common fivefold liability rule—suggesting the text treats verbal and physical violence as analogous juridical categories governed by the same underlying logic.

themes.topic: Spies and intelligence operations as tools of criminal justice

mentions.quote: Having identified them through very skillful spies who practice the same trade, they should be pursued and caught by men who are secretly deployed
other trustworthy and clever-speaking spies, who were formerly thieves, should be deployed; they should incite those thieves
Assembly halls, watering places, cake shops, brothels, places selling liquor and food, crossroads, sacred trees, public gatherings, and spectacles

themes.justification: Section 19 devotes several verses to an organised intelligence apparatus—using reformed thieves as undercover agents, specifying surveillance venues, and describing sting operations—revealing a sophisticated state security methodology implicit in the Dharmaśāstra tradition.

themes.topic: Gambling as a regulated, state-supervised institution

mentions.quote: The keeper of the gambling house should arrange the game and should pay what is due from it. A tenth part of a hundred shall be his profit
Gamblers should rely on other gamblers in case of a dispute. They themselves shall be the investigators of it
The king should banish from the gambling circle those sinful men who play with false dice

themes.justification: Chapter 17 frames gambling not as a blanket prohibition but as a legally regulated activity with prescribed house-keeper obligations, internal dispute resolution, and royal enforcement against cheating—treating it as an institution analogous to commerce.

citations.quote: the punishment is death. For a lesser amount, he should be made to pay a fine of eleven times the value, so said Manu
citations.justification: Manu is directly quoted as the source for the specific grain-theft penalty, positioning the Manusmṛti as a prior authoritative text whose rulings the Nāradasmṛti endorses and incorporates.

citations.quote: With whatever particular limb a thief operates, that very limb of his should be cut off; this is the ordinance of Manu
citations.justification: The lex talionis-style mutilation rule is attributed to Manu's ordinance, treating the Manusmṛti as a legislative source whose authority the Nāradasmṛti explicitly cites.

citations.quote: Manu Svāyaṃbhuva declared ten places of punishment, which should apply to the three classes; a Brāhmaṇa is always protected
citations.justification: Manu Svāyaṃbhuva is named as the declarer of the ten bodily sites of punishment, directly attributing this juridical classification to his authority.

citations.quote: A perpetrator of violence, who has abandoned his own self, should not be released by the king because of friendship or a large monetary gain, said Manu
citations.justification: Manu is cited as the authority against releasing violent offenders, reinforcing the Manusmṛti's standing as a parallel legal text whose rulings the Nāradasmṛti endorses.

citations.quote: the ordeal is known to be of five kinds, so says the blessed Manu
citations.justification: Manu is invoked as the authority for the fivefold typology of ordeals, situating the ordeal chapter within a shared Dharmaśāstra tradition.

citations.quote: This threefold punishment for crimes of violence was declared by the Self-existent One
citations.justification: The epithet 'Self-existent One' (Svāyaṃbhuva) refers to Manu Svāyaṃbhuva, who is cited as the authority for the three-tier amercement scale for violent crime.

citations.quote: For a Brāhmaṇa, it is sixty-fourfold; thus said Svāyaṃbhuva
citations.justification: Svāyaṃbhuva (Manu) is credited with the graduated theft-sin multiplier table, again treating the Manusmṛti as the source text being cited.
